summary.text: A cotangent–Fourier identity expresses the mirror difference \(\sum_k(-k^2\bmod n)-\sum_k(k^2\bmod n)\) as a divisor sum of local terms, whose nonnegativity follows from quadratic Gauss-sum evaluations in the residue classes modulo \(4\) together with positivity of the associated odd-character cotangent sums. Thus the original sum is at most its mirror, while the two sums together are at most \(n(n-1)\); integrality and parity then give the stated half-square bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
e(x)=e^{2\pi i x},\qquad
G(m,q)=\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}e\!\left(\frac{mk^2}{q}\right)
\]
for positive integers \(q\), and put
\[
\operatorname{cot}_q(m)=\frac{\cos(\pi m/q)}{\sin(\pi m/q)}
=\cot\left(\frac{\pi m}{q}\right)\qquad(1\le m<q).
\]
We will prove the result by comparing the sum of the least nonnegative quadratic residues with the corresponding sum for their negatives.

For a positive integer \(n\), write
\[
A(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(k^2\bmod n),
\qquad
A^-(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}((-k^2)\bmod n),
\]
where every residue is represented in \(\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}\). Thus
\[
(-k^2)\bmod n=(n-(k^2\bmod n))\bmod n.
\]
The sequence in the question equals \(A(n)\): replacing the index set \(1,\dots,n\) by \(0,\dots,n-1\) merely replaces the term \(n^2\bmod n=0\) by \(0^2\bmod n=0\).

The central goal is to prove
\[
A(n)\le A^-(n). \tag{1}
\]
We first establish the analytic and arithmetic ingredients needed for this comparison.


1. A finite cotangent kernel

For \(0\le a<n\), we claim
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\cot\left(\frac{\pi m}{n}\right)
 \sin\left(\frac{2\pi am}{n}\right)
=
\begin{cases}
0,&a=0,\\
n-2a,&1\le a<n.
\end{cases} \tag{2}
\]

To prove this, first note the elementary trigonometric identity
\[
\cot\theta\,\sin(2a\theta)
=2\sum_{j=0}^{a}\cos(2j\theta)-1-\cos(2a\theta), \tag{3}
\]
valid when \(\sin\theta\ne0\). It follows by induction on \(a\), using the addition formulas for sine and cosine; equivalently, the difference between the formulas for \(a+1\) and \(a\) is the standard product-to-sum identity.

We also use the complete root-of-unity sum
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}e^{2\pi i jm/n}
=
\begin{cases}
n,&n\mid j,\\0,&n\nmid j.
\end{cases}
\]
Taking real parts gives
\[
\sum_{m=0}^{n-1}\cos(2\pi jm/n)
=
\begin{cases}
n,&n\mid j,\\0,&n\nmid j.
\end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
For \(0\le j<n\), subtracting the \(m=0\) term shows that the sum over \(1\le m<n\) is \(n-1\) if \(j=0\), and \(-1\) otherwise. Summing (3), with \(\theta=\pi m/n\), over \(m=1,\dots,n-1\), and applying (4), gives (2). Notice that \(0<\pi m/n<\pi\), so the denominators in (3) do not vanish.

The imaginary part of the Gauss sum is
\[
\Im G(m,n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
 \sin\left(\frac{2\pi m(k^2\bmod n)}{n}\right). \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, replacing \(k^2\) by its remainder modulo \(n\) changes the argument of \(e(x)\) by an integer.

Multiply (5) by \(\operatorname{cot}_n(m)\), sum over \(1\le m<n\), and interchange the two finite sums. Applying (2) with \(a=k^2\bmod n\), each \(k\) contributes \(0\) when that remainder is zero, and otherwise contributes
\[
n-2(k^2\bmod n)
=(( -k^2)\bmod n)-(k^2\bmod n).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{cot}_n(m)\Im G(m,n)
=A^-(n)-A(n).} \tag{6}
\]


2. Decomposition according to the gcd

For \(q\ge2\), define the local sum
\[
V(q)=\sum_{\substack{1\le m<q\\(m,q)=1}}
\operatorname{cot}_q(m)\Im G(m,q). \tag{7}
\]
We claim that
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\operatorname{cot}_n(m)\Im G(m,n)
=
\sum_{\substack{q\mid n\\q>1}}\frac nq\,V(q). \tag{8}
\]

Every \(m\) with \(1\le m<n\) has a unique representation
\[
g=(m,n),\qquad q=n/g,
\qquad m'=m/g,
\]
where \(q\mid n\), \(q>1\), \(1\le m'<q\), and \((m',q)=1\). Conversely, such a pair \((q,m')\) gives \(m=(n/q)m'\). Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{cot}_n(m)=\operatorname{cot}_q(m'). \tag{9}
\]
The summand in the Gauss sum is periodic modulo \(q\), and the range of length \(n\) consists of \(n/q\) complete periods. More explicitly, since \(m/n=m'/q\),
\[
G(m,n)=\frac nq\,G(m',q). \tag{10}
\]
Equations (9) and (10), followed by the above bijective grouping of the indices, prove (8).

Thus (1) will follow from
\[
V(q)\ge0\qquad(q\ge2). \tag{11}
\]
The rest of the proof establishes (11).


3. Positivity of cotangent sums for real odd characters

We need the following general lemma.

Lemma. Let \(q\ge2\), and let \(\psi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R\) satisfy
\[
\psi(r+q)=\psi(r),\qquad
\psi(ab)=\psi(a)\psi(b),\qquad
|\psi(a)|\le1,
\]
and
\[
\psi(a)=-\psi(b)\quad\text{whenever }a+b=q.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\psi(m)\cot\left(\frac{\pi m}{q}\right)\ge0. \tag{12}
\]

Proof. First, periodicity and oddness imply \(\psi(0)=0\), and pairing \(m\) with \(q-m\) gives
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\psi(m)=0. \tag{13}
\]
If \(\psi(1)\ne1\), complete multiplicativity gives
\(\psi(1)^2=\psi(1)\), hence \(\psi(1)=0\). Then
\(\psi(m)=\psi(m)\psi(1)=0\) for every \(m\), and (12) is immediate. We may therefore assume \(\psi(1)=1\).

For real \(s\) and integers \(j\ge0\), define the block
\[
C_j(s)=\sum_{a=1}^{q-1}\psi(a)(jq+a)^{-s}. \tag{14}
\]
For \(s>1\), absolute convergence permits grouping the Dirichlet series into these blocks:
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}C_j(s)
=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{\psi(r)}{r^s}. \tag{15}
\]
Complete multiplicativity gives the Euler product
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{\psi(r)}{r^s}
=\prod_p\left(1-\frac{\psi(p)}{p^s}\right)^{-1}. \tag{16}
\]
Each factor is positive: since \(|\psi(p)|\le1\) and \(p^{-s}<1\), one has \(1-\psi(p)p^{-s}>0\). Finite partial products are therefore nonnegative, and passage to their convergent limit gives
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}C_j(s)\ge0\qquad(s>1). \tag{17}
\]

We now pass to \(s=1\). For \(1\le s\le2\), equation (13) lets us subtract the constant \((jq+q)^{-s}\) from every term of a block. For \(j\ge1\), this yields
\[
C_j(s)=\sum_{a=1}^{q-1}\psi(a) igl((jq+a)^{-s}-(jq+q)^{-s}\bigr).
\]
An elementary estimate gives
\[
|C_j(s)|\le \frac{2}{j^2}. \tag{18}
\]
For completeness, if \(u=jq+a\), \(v=jq+q\), then \(1\le u\le v\), and for \(1\le s\le2\),
\[
u^{-s}-v^{-s}
\le \frac{(v-u)(v+u)}{u v^2}.
\]
This follows by writing
\[
u^{-s}-v^{-s}=u^{-s}\bigl(1-(u/v)^s\bigr),
\]
using \(u^{-s}\le u^{-1}\) and, because \(0<u/v\le1\) and \(s\le2\),
\((u/v)^2\le(u/v)^s\). Since \(v-u\le q\), \(v+u\le2v\), and \(u,v\ge jq\), summing over the fewer than \(q\) possible values of \(a\) gives (18). Also \(|C_0(s)|\le q\). Thus the blocks are dominated, uniformly for \(1<s\le2\), by a summable sequence. Since each finite block is continuous in \(s\), dominated convergence in (17) gives
\[
L:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}C_j(1)\ge0. \tag{19}
\]

It remains to identify this limit with the cotangent sum. The partial-fraction expansion of the cotangent says, for \(0<x<1\),
\[
\pi\cot(\pi x)-\frac1x
=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}
\left(\frac1{x+r+1}+\frac1{x-r-1}\right). \tag{20}
\]
This follows, for example, by pairing the positive and negative terms in the standard Mittag-Leffler expansion
\(\pi\cot(\pi x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(x+k)^{-1}\).
Taking \(x=m/q\) and dividing by \(q\), (20) becomes
\[
\frac\pi q\operatorname{cot}_q(m)-\frac1m
=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}
\left(
\frac1{m+(r+1)q}-\frac1{(r+1)q-m}
\right). \tag{21}
\]
Multiply by \(\psi(m)\), sum over \(m=1,\dots,q-1\), and in the second part replace \(m\) by \(q-m\). Oddness of \(\psi\) shows that the \(r\)-th sum on the right is
\[
C_{r+1}(1)+C_r(1).
\]
The sum of the left side is
\[
\frac\pi q\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\psi(m)\operatorname{cot}_q(m)-C_0(1).
\]
Since \(\sum C_j(1)\) converges absolutely by (18), summing over \(r\) gives
\[
\frac\pi q\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\psi(m)\operatorname{cot}_q(m)-C_0(1)
=2L-C_0(1).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\psi(m)\operatorname{cot}_q(m)
=\frac{2q}{\pi}L\ge0,
\]
proving the lemma. \(\square\)

A useful consequence is the following. Suppose, in addition, that \(\psi(m)=0\) whenever \((m,q)>1\), and that for all \((m,q)=1\),
\[
\Im G(m,q)=c\psi(m) \tag{22}
\]
with \(c\ge0\). Then
\[
V(q)=c\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\psi(m)\operatorname{cot}_q(m)\ge0. \tag{23}
\]


4. Quadratic Gauss-sum formulas

We record and justify the formulas used to put \(\Im G(m,q)\) into the form (22).

First, for every positive \(N\),
\[
G(1,N)=\frac{(1+i)(1+(-i)^N)}2\sqrt N. \tag{24}
\]
Here is a derivation. Let
\[
\Theta(z,\tau)=\sum_{r\in\mathbb Z}
 e^{\pi i(r^2\tau+2rz)},\qquad \Im\tau>0.
\]
Poisson summation applied to the Gaussian gives the Jacobi transformation
\[
\Theta(z,\tau)=(-i\tau)^{-1/2}
 e^{-\pi i z^2/\tau}\Theta(z/\tau,-1/\tau), \tag{25}
\]
with the principal square root. Splitting the defining series into residue classes modulo \(M\) and then applying (25) to each inner series gives, whenever \(M^2c\) is an even integer and \(Mc\) is an integer,
\[
\Theta(0,c+w)=
\frac1{(-iM^2w)^{1/2}}
\sum_{r=0}^{M-1}e^{\pi i r^2c}
\Theta\left(\frac rM,-\frac1{M^2w}\right). \tag{26}
\]
Take \(c=2/N\), \(M=N\), and \(w=it\), where \(t>0\). This expresses \(\Theta(0,2/N+it)\) as \((N\sqrt t)^{-1}\) times a finite sum \(S_1(t)\). Apply (25) to the left side and note the exact identity
\[
-\frac1{2/N+it}=-\frac N2+\frac{iNt}{2(2/N+it)}.
\]
Now apply (26) a second time, with \(M=2\), to the theta function at this latter point. One obtains
\[
S_1(t)=C(t)S_2(t),
\]
where
\[
C(t)=
\frac{N}{(-i(2/N+it))^{1/2}
\bigl((2N)/(2/N+it)\bigr)^{1/2}}.
\]
As \(t\downarrow0\), the imaginary parts of the transformed theta parameters tend to \(+\infty\). Since
\[
\Theta(x,iT)\longrightarrow1\qquad(T\to+\infty)

after the harmless real shifts occurring here, the two finite sums tend respectively to
\[
S_1(t)\longrightarrow
\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i r^2/N}=G(1,N),
\]
and
\[
S_2(t)\longrightarrow1+(-i)^N.
\]
(The convergence follows directly by bounding the nonzero terms by the geometric majorant \(2e^{-\pi T}/(1-e^{-\pi T})\).)
Finally, evaluating the principal square roots in \(C(t)\) as \(t\downarrow0\), using
\[
(-i)^{1/2}=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}(1-i),
\]
gives the coefficient \((1+i)\sqrt N/2\), and hence (24).

In particular, for odd \(w\),
\[
G(1,w)=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt w,&w\equiv1\pmod4,\\
i\sqrt w,&w\equiv3\pmod4.
\end{cases} \tag{27}
\]

For odd \(q\) and \((m,q)=1\), one has
\[
G(m,q)=\left(\frac mq\right)G(1,q), \tag{28}
\]
where \((\frac mq)\) is the Jacobi symbol. We briefly supply the arithmetic proof. For an odd prime \(p\), count the solutions of \(x^2=a\) modulo \(p\): the number is \(1+\left(\frac ap\right)\). Grouping \(G(m,p)\) by \(a=x^2\) and using the fact that a nontrivial additive character sums to zero gives
\[
G(m,p)=\sum_{a\bmod p}\left(\frac ap\right)e(ma/p).
\]
Multiplication by \(m\) permutes the nonzero residues, and multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol therefore gives
\(G(m,p)=(\frac mp)G(1,p)\).
For odd prime powers, splitting an index modulo \(p^{d+2}\) as
\(x+p^{d+1}j\), and summing first over \(j\bmod p\), shows
\[
G(m,p^{d+2})=pG(m,p^d) \qquad(p\nmid m). \tag{29}
\]
Indeed, the inner geometric sum vanishes unless \(p\mid x\), after which replacing \(x\) by \(py\) gives (29). This proves (28) for prime powers by induction. Finally, if \((A,B)=1\), the Chinese remainder parametrization gives
\[
G(m,AB)=G(mB,A)G(mA,B). \tag{30}
\]
Combining (30), quadratic reciprocity as encoded by the multiplicativity of the Jacobi symbol, and the prime-power result proves (28) for every odd \(q\).

We also need powers of two. Direct summation gives, for odd \(m\),
\[
G(m,2)=0,
\quad G(m,4)=2(1+i^m),
\quad G(m,8)=4e(m/8). \tag{31}
\]
Splitting into two equal blocks and using a geometric sum gives the recursion
\[
G(m,2^{d+4})=2G(m,2^{d+2})\qquad(m\text{ odd}). \tag{32}
\]
For example, write an index as \(x+2^{d+2}j\), \(j=0,1\). The inner sum is zero unless \(x\) is even; after writing \(x=2y\), it becomes twice the sum at modulus \(2^{d+2}\). From (31) and (32),
\[
G(m,2^{2k+2})=2^{k+1}(1+i^m), \tag{33}
\]
\[
G(m,2^{2k+3})=2^{k+2}e(m/8). \tag{34}
\]


5. The characters needed in the case analysis

Let
\[
\chi_4(r)=
\begin{cases}1&r\equiv1\pmod4,\\-1&r\equiv3\pmod4,\\0&r\text{ even},\end{cases}
\]
\[
\chi_8(r)=
\begin{cases}1&r\equiv1,7\pmod8,\\-1&r\equiv3,5\pmod8,\\0&r\text{ even},\end{cases}
\]
and
\[
\chi'_8(r)=
\begin{cases}1&r\equiv1,3\pmod8,\\-1&r\equiv5,7\pmod8,\\0&r\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]
Also let \(\chi_{\rm odd}(r)=1\) for odd \(r\), and \(0\) for even \(r\). Direct multiplication of residue classes shows that all four functions are completely multiplicative and bounded in absolute value by \(1\). We shall use
\[
i^r=\chi_4(r)i\quad(r\text{ odd}), \tag{35}
\]
and
\[
e(r/8)=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\bigl(\chi_8(r)+i\chi'_8(r)\bigr)
\quad(r\text{ odd}). \tag{36}
\]
For odd \(w\), let \(J_w(r)=(\frac rw)\). It is completely multiplicative, periodic modulo \(w\), bounded by \(1\), and vanishes exactly when \((r,w)>1\). Furthermore,
\[
J_w(-r)=
\begin{cases}
J_w(r),&w\equiv1\pmod4,\\
-J_w(r),&w\equiv3\pmod4,
\end{cases} \tag{37}
\]
and
\[
J_w(2)=\chi_8(w). \tag{38}
\]
All these statements follow directly from the standard supplementary laws for the Jacobi symbol.


6. Proof that \(V(q)\ge0\)

We divide into residue classes modulo \(4\).

If \(q\) is odd, equations (27) and (28) give, for \((m,q)=1\),
\[
G(m,q)=J_q(m)G(1,q).
\]
If \(q\equiv1\pmod4\), this is real, so every term in (7) has zero imaginary part and
\[
V(q)=0. \tag{39}
\]
If \(q\equiv3\pmod4\), then
\[
\Im G(m,q)=\sqrt q\,J_q(m).
\]
The function \(J_q\) is periodic modulo \(q\), completely multiplicative, bounded by \(1\), vanishes off the coprime residues, and is odd under \(m\mapsto q-m\) by (37). Thus (23), with \(c=\sqrt q\), gives \(V(q)\ge0\).

If \(q\equiv2\pmod4\), write \(q=2w\), with \(w\) odd. Every \(m\) coprime to \(q\) is odd. By (30),
\[
G(m,2w)=G(mw,2)G(2m,w)=0
\]
by (31), so again
\[
V(q)=0. \tag{40}
\]

It remains to treat \(4\mid q\). Write uniquely
\[
q=2^Ew,
\qquad w\text{ odd},\quad E\ge2. \tag{41}
\]
For \((m,q)=1\), both \(m\) and \(mw\) are odd. Chinese-remainder multiplicativity gives
\[
G(m,q)=G(mw,2^E)G(m2^E,w). \tag{42}
\]
By (28),
\[
G(m2^E,w)=J_w(m2^E)G(1,w)
=J_w(m)J_w(2)^E G(1,w). \tag{43}
\]
We now split according to the parity of \(E\) and the class of \(w\) modulo \(4\).

Suppose first that \(E=2k+2\) is even. Then (33), (35), and (43) apply, and \(J_w(2)^E=1\).

If \(w\equiv1\pmod4\), then \(G(1,w)=\sqrt w\) and \(\chi_4(w)=1\). Thus
\[
\Im G(m,q)=2^{k+1}\sqrt w\,\chi_4(m)J_w(m). \tag{44}
\]
Take \(\psi(m)=\chi_4(m)J_w(m)\). It is periodic modulo \(q\), because \(4\mid q\) and \(w\mid q\); it is completely multiplicative and bounded by \(1\). It vanishes when \((m,q)>1\): either \(m\) is even, when \(\chi_4(m)=0\), or \((m,w)>1\), when \(J_w(m)=0\). Finally, under \(m\mapsto q-m\), \(\chi_4\) changes sign while \(J_w\) does not, by (37). Hence \(\psi\) is odd, and (23), with the nonnegative coefficient \(2^{k+1}\sqrt w\), proves \(V(q)\ge0\).

If \(w\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(G(1,w)=i\sqrt w\). Multiplying \(1+i^{mw}\) by \(i\), its imaginary part is \(1\). Therefore
\[
\Im G(m,q)=2^{k+1}\sqrt w\,J_w(m) \tag{45}
\]
for coprime \(m\). To define a function on all integers which also vanishes off the coprime residues, take
\(\psi(m)=\chi_{\rm odd}(m)J_w(m)\). It is periodic and multiplicative, and it vanishes if \(m\) is even or is not coprime to \(w\). The parity factor is unchanged by reflection modulo the even number \(q\), while \(J_w\) changes sign because \(w\equiv3\pmod4\). Thus \(\psi\) is odd. Equation (45) and (23) again give \(V(q)\ge0\).

Now suppose that \(E=2k+3\) is odd. From (34), (36), (38), and (43), the common nonnegative scalar in the imaginary-part formulas is
\[
c=2^{k+2}\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\sqrt w. \tag{46}
\]

If \(w\equiv1\pmod4\), then \(G(1,w)=\sqrt w\). Since
\[
J_w(2)^E=\chi_8(w)
\]
and a check of the two possibilities \(w\equiv1,5\pmod8\) gives
\[
\chi'_8(w)\chi_8(w)=1,
\]
the multiplicativity of \(\chi'_8\) shows
\[
\Im G(m,q)=c\,\chi'_8(m)J_w(m). \tag{47}
\]
Take \(\psi=\chi'_8J_w\). It is periodic modulo \(q\), multiplicative, bounded, and vanishes off the coprime residues. Since \(8\mid q\), \(\chi'_8(q-m)=-\chi'_8(m)\), while \(J_w(q-m)=J_w(m)\) because \(w\equiv1\pmod4\). Thus it is odd, and (23) applies.

If \(w\equiv3\pmod4\), multiplication by \(G(1,w)=i\sqrt w\) makes the real component of \(e(mw/8)\) contribute to the imaginary part. Since \(\chi_8\) is multiplicative and \(\chi_8(w)^2=1\), we obtain
\[
\Im G(m,q)=c\,\chi_8(m)J_w(m). \tag{48}
\]
Take \(\psi=\chi_8J_w\). Reflection modulo a multiple of \(8\) leaves \(\chi_8\) unchanged, whereas (37) changes the sign of \(J_w\). Thus this \(\psi\) is again an odd, periodic, completely multiplicative function, bounded by \(1\) and vanishing off the coprime residues. Equation (23) proves \(V(q)\ge0\).

The four subcases cover every factorization (41), and together with (39) and (40) prove (11) for every \(q\ge2\).


7. Completion of the inequality

Combining (6), (8), and the just-proved nonnegativity of every \(V(q)\), we obtain
\[
A^-(n)-A(n)
=\sum_{\substack{q\mid n\\q>1}}\frac nq V(q)\ge0.
\]
This proves (1): \(A(n)\le A^-(n)\).

For each \(k\), put \(r=k^2\bmod n\). If \(r=0\), then
\[
r+(-r\bmod n)=0;
\]
if \(r\ne0\), then \((-r\bmod n)=n-r\), so the sum is \(n\). In particular, the term with \(k=0\) contributes zero, and every one of the other \(n-1\) terms contributes at most \(n\). Therefore
\[
A(n)+A^-(n)\le n(n-1). \tag{49}
\]
Together with \(A(n)\le A^-(n)\), this yields
\[
2A(n)\le A(n)+A^-(n)\le n(n-1). \tag{50}
\]
For \(n\ge1\),
\[
n(n-1)=n^2-n\le n^2-1.
\]
Hence
\[
2A(n)\le n^2-1.
\]
Because \(A(n)\) is an integer, this is equivalent to
\[
A(n)\le \left\lfloor\frac{n^2-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
The quotient in the statement is integer division, i.e. precisely this floor. Since \(A(n)=a(n)\), we conclude that for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
\boxed{a(n)\le\frac{n^2-1}{2}}.
\]
